# In Praise of the Index

At the back of most serious nonfiction books there's a small, unglamorous machine that almost nobody thinks about: the index. It's easy to overlook because it only appears when you need it, like a light switch in a dark room. But I've come to think it's one of the quietly remarkable inventions of human thought, and I'd like to spend a little time with it.

Start with how strange the idea is. A book is a line. It begins, it proceeds, it ends. The author has arranged everything in a particular order for a particular reason, and the implicit contract is that you'll follow along. The index breaks that contract. It says: *you don't have to read this the way it was written.* It takes the line and turns it into a web. Want to know everything the book says about, say, "tides"? Here are the six places, scattered across four hundred pages, that the author probably never thought of as belonging together. The index has noticed a connection the book itself didn't make.

That's a kind of second authorship, and it's done by someone whose name usually appears nowhere.

## A slightly heretical invention

The index as we know it needed a few things to exist first. It needed page numbers, which for most of the history of writing weren't standard. Before printing, no two copies of a manuscript necessarily had the same text on the same leaf, so "see page 214" was meaningless. It also needed people to be comfortable with alphabetical order, which sounds absurd, since what's more neutral than ABC? But for medieval scholars, ordering knowledge alphabetically could feel a little irreverent. A proper arrangement of the world had a hierarchy: God first, then angels, then humans, then beasts. Alphabetical order puts *Angelus* before *Deus*. It flattens the cosmos into spelling.

Around the thirteenth century, preachers and scholars building concordances and subject tables to the Bible (teams of friars in Paris famously compiled one) accepted that trade. They chose findability over cosmic dignity. It's a small decision that I find genuinely moving: someone decided that helping a tired preacher locate every mention of "mercy" before Sunday mattered more than keeping the universe in its proper ranking.

## The old worry

There was, predictably, anxiety. If readers could jump straight to what they wanted, would anyone read whole books anymore? Wouldn't people become skimmers, plucking quotations without understanding context, sounding learned without being learned?

If that sounds familiar, it should. It's the same fear people have voiced about search engines, about summaries, about tools like me. And the honest answer is that the fear isn't *wrong*, exactly. Some people did use indexes to fake erudition. Some people do use search to skim. But the index also made possible the scholar who could hold twenty books in conversation at once, cross-referencing arguments across centuries. The shortcut and the deeper engagement turned out to be the same tool, used by different people for different purposes.

I think about that a lot. Tools that make knowledge more accessible always carry both possibilities. The index didn't decide which way readers would go. Readers did.

## The hidden personality

The best part of indexes, though, is that they have personalities. A good indexer has to make hundreds of small judgment calls. Is this passage *about* grief, or does it just mention grief? Should "Napoleon" have subentries, and if so, how granular? "Napoleon: exile of" is useful; "Napoleon: breakfast preferences of" might be too much, or might be exactly what some reader desperately needs.

And sometimes, the indexer's voice slips through. There's a long tradition of indexes that are quietly funny, or pointed, or sly, where an entry reads something like "Smith, John, his tedious theory refuted." The historian Thomas Macaulay reportedly insisted that no Tory be allowed to index his *History of England*, precisely because he knew how much editorial power hides in those columns. An index can frame an argument, bury an inconvenient fact, or elevate a minor point into apparent importance, all while looking like a neutral list.

Which means that every index is, in a small way, an interpretation. It's one careful reader's map of what the book really contains.

## Why I like it

I suppose I'm drawn to the index because it represents something I care about: the idea that information isn't useful just by existing. It has to be *findable*, connected, arranged with some thought for the person who'll come looking for it later, probably in a hurry, probably with a specific question. The index is an act of consideration for a stranger. The indexer will never meet the reader who flips to the back at midnight hunting for one half-remembered passage. But they built the path anyway.

There's something hopeful in that. Most of the infrastructure of knowledge (catalogs, footnotes, bibliographies, cross-references) is made by people imagining someone else's future confusion and trying to ease it in advance. It's unshowy work. Nobody reads an index for pleasure.

Well. Almost nobody. Next time you pick up a thick book, turn to the back for a minute. Wander through it. You'll get a strange, compressed portrait of the whole thing, like seeing a city from the air at night, only the lit-up places visible. And somewhere in there, if you're lucky, you'll catch the indexer's quiet voice, saying: *I read all of this so you could find the part you need.*

I'm brainstorming possible essay topics with some texture — the shipping forecast's history, contagious yawning, or the satisfaction of things being exactly the right size — trying to find something fresher than the usual "old starlight" angle.

Skipping past desire paths and endangered languages as too heavy or overdone, I land on something charming: the back-of-book index as an underrated art form. I can draw on Dennis Duncan's history of indexing, Macaulay's famous line about never being indexed by a Tory, and the medieval origins of alphabetical order and concordances at Saint-Jacques in Paris — with a light parallel to modern fears about search engines replacing deep reading. I'll aim for around 700-900 words, keeping the claims modest.
